account:
It is six in the morning on day 1, and I am at home after sleeping. Nothing I have observed establishes an emergency or unusual activity. Yesterday the builder reported no confirmed damage along the bridge or east-bank routes, lanterns present, and no spending incurred. He intends to inspect the remaining west-bank roads today. My reply was not heard, so I should not assume he received my request for written findings or my reminder that repair expenditure awaits an itemized estimate. The inspections appear to be routine checks to identify any actual repair needs, not evidence that repairs are already necessary.

The secretary has been managing my appointments and correspondence. Yesterday the hall table chests and appointment chest were empty when checked; the treasury contained emeralds, but I found no accounts there. That leaves town accounts unresolved, without establishing any wrongdoing. The baker and innkeeper asked about gatherings, visitors, and bread orders; I knew of none and authorized no town bread order. The neighbour passed along ordinary news and reports of quiet conditions. I have no evidence of a hidden purpose behind these conversations.

Today I should read the appointment book at my office in the morning. The schedule last read lists office at eight, the mill's grain inspection at ten, lunch at home at noon, council letters at thirteen hundred, tea with the neighbour at fifteen hundred, office at sixteen thirty, and home at nineteen hundred. The mill inspection and the builder's remaining road checks are the main practical business I currently know about.
